summary: Proposes experimental congestion control algorithms for multipath transport such as Multipath TCP. Using several paths at once is more efficient, but single-path algorithms do not suit it, so the paths' congestion control must be coupled. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: If you open several roads at once, the drivers must coordinate so they do not all jam the same one. This gives Multipath TCP a way to share load fairly and avoid traffic jams.

questions: what is the linked increases algorithm
what is alpha in mptcp congestion control
what is the mptcp traffic shifting attack
subtitle: A congestion control algorithm that couples the subflows of a multipath connection so it is fair to ordinary TCP.

tldr.problem: Running standard TCP congestion control independently on each subflow gives a multipath flow more than its fair share when subflows share a bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: The Linked Increases algorithm couples the additive increase of the subflows through a parameter alpha, while using unmodified TCP behavior on a drop.
tldr.outcome: The multipath flow is fair to TCP at bottlenecks and shifts some traffic away from congested paths, though it does not achieve full resource pooling.

facts.label: Recommended alpha_scale
facts.value: 512 (works well in a wide range of scenarios)

today: RFC 6356 is Experimental and has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata. It extends the standard TCP congestion control of RFC 5681 for multipath use.

sections.title: The Problem with Many Paths
sections.content:
Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is a set of extensions to regular TCP that lets one connection be spread across multiple paths, using separate subflows. Each subflow needs its own congestion window (cwnd) so that offered load matches capacity on that path.

The simplest approach is to run standard TCP congestion control on each subflow. The RFC calls this unsatisfactory: it gives the multipath flow an unfair share when its subflows cross a common bottleneck.
sections.plainLanguage: If you split your shopping across three checkout lanes and each lane lets you go as fast as a single shopper, you take three people's share of the store's attention.

sections.title: Three Goals
sections.content:
The RFC states three goals for a practical multipath congestion controller:

  • Goal 1, improve throughput: a multipath flow should perform at least as well as a single-path flow on the best of its paths.
  • Goal 2, do no harm: it should not take more capacity from any shared resource than a single flow using only one of its paths.
  • Goal 3, balance congestion: it should move as much traffic as possible off its most congested paths, subject to the first two goals.

Goals 1 and 2 together ensure fairness at the bottleneck. Goal 3 is the idea of resource pooling, which is achieved by coupling the congestion control loops of the subflows.
sections.plainLanguage: Be at least as fast as your best road, do not hog more than one driver would, and drift toward the emptier roads.

sections.title: The Linked Increases Algorithm
sections.content:
The algorithm changes only the increase phase of congestion avoidance. Slow start, fast retransmit, fast recovery and the multiplicative decrease are the same as in standard TCP (RFC 5681).

For each ACK on subflow i, cwnd_i is increased by the minimum of two values: alpha * bytes_acked * MSS_i / cwnd_total, and bytes_acked * MSS_i / cwnd_i. The second value is what TCP would get, so a subflow is never more aggressive than a single TCP flow. If the increase rounds to 0, it MUST be set to 1.

The parameter alpha sets the aggressiveness of the whole flow. It is computed from the observed windows and round-trip times as cwnd_total * MAX(cwnd_i/rtt_i^2) / (SUM(cwnd_i/rtt_i))^2, so that the total throughput equals what TCP would get on the best path.

When computing cwnd_total, a subflow in fast retransmit should contribute its ssthresh rather than its inflated cwnd. For app-limited connections the computation should take the minimum with flight_size_i.
sections.plainLanguage: Each road may speed up a little, but never faster than a lone driver would, and the total speed is tuned to match the best single road.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The formula for alpha involves floating point, which is costly per ACK and disabled in many kernels. The RFC suggests an integer version using an alpha_scale that is a small power of two. Its experiments show alpha_scale=512 works well in a wide range of scenarios. Larger values increase precision but also the risk of overflow, which 64-bit operations would avoid.

Implementations MAY keep a per-connection cwnd_total variable. Alpha can be a per-connection variable, computed on each drop and once per RTT otherwise, or even once per drop if an average RTT per sawtooth is used.

For stacks that count the window in packets, the RFC gives a change using a per-subflow cwnd_cnt_i and a rearranged alpha formula, and notes that MSS rarely differs between paths in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers do whole-number math faster than fractions, so the recipe is rewritten to avoid fractions, and the answer is only updated now and then.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Security
sections.content:
The algorithm fully achieves Goals 1 and 2 but not full resource pooling. Perfect pooling needs both increase and decrease to be coupled, as in a fully coupled controller. The RFC says such controllers insufficiently probe paths with high loss rates and show "flappiness", putting all the window on one random subflow and flipping between them.

By coupling only the increases, this design keeps probing lossy paths and avoids flappiness. The window ends up allocated so that p_i * cwnd_i is constant across subflows, so a lower-loss path gets progressively more window.

For security, the RFC describes a traffic-shifting attack: an on-path attacker drops packets on one subflow so the sender pushes more data onto other paths. The effect is minor, since at worst a subflow becomes as aggressive as one TCP flow, but the new path may see all of the traffic. The RFC advises that end-to-end encryption, not multipath, is the answer when privacy is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The roads are not shared perfectly, but this way drivers keep checking every road and do not all stampede onto one at random.
